html:
The Bois Caiman ceremony was a Vodou gathering held in a forest in northern Saint-Domingue in August 1791. Led by Dutty Boukman and the priestess Cecile Fatiman, enslaved people swore to rise against their masters.

About a week later the revolt broke out on the plantations of the northern plain, the start of the Haitian Revolution. Boukman was killed within months.

Historians debate the details, which come from later accounts. But in Haitian memory Bois Caiman is the birth of the nation, and it shows the role of African faith in the revolt. Some foreign preachers have cited it to attack Haiti and Vodou, as a pact with evil, which Haitians reject.
